newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - Printronix in Asian expansion.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Printronix in Asian expansion.

text.p: Printronix Inc aims to clinch 40 percent of the market share in China, Taiwan and South Korea over the next five years, its chief executive officer said on Wednesday.

Robert Kleist, also the president of the maker of business and industrial printers, told Reuters in a telephone interview the group's Chinese-language printers were strategic to this growth and would help it make inroads into China, where its presence was now "insignificant".
Kleist, one of the founders of Printronix, was in Singapore to launch the company's Chinese language printers.
"Having a Kanji (Chinese character) printer and entering the Chinese market is very strategic to us," Kleist said.

"Today about eight percent of our total worldwide revenue comes from the Asia Pacific market. We think with this product over the next five years, we would be able to grow our Asia Pacific business to about 30 percent of our worldwide business."
India, Pakistan and Vietnam were also among the company's target markets, he said.
Printronix's net income for the nine months ended December 1996 was at US$8.13 million on a turnover of US$132.33 million.
Given the region's growing importance, Kleist said the Kanji models would be expanded for applications in Korea and Taiwan.
"The product line that we have announced is the first step that we are taking and we are developing a broader range of printing speed besides developing more language capability," he said.
Its Singapore operations would play a key role in the group's Asian warpath, Kleist said.
"The Singapore facility will also be the regional headquarters and will support any expansion of manufacturing within Asia Pacific as needed for a growing market presence," Kleist said.

Printronix's S$16 million manufacturing plant in Singapore produces about half the company's global output of 8,000 line printers every quarter. Its Irvine, California, plant accounts for the other half.

Kleist said there were no immediate plans to build new manufacturing plants elsewhere though China could prove to be the next logical location. But this could be another two years down the road assuming sales justify the move, he said.
Kleist said the company would use internal funds to finance its expansion plans. The company has about US$11 million in cash, he added.
Kleist, who holds about 16 percent of the company's shares, dismissed rumours that he intends to sell his stake.
He said analysts had projected the company's sales for the year ended March 1997 would be over US$175 million against US$159 million previously.
